captions.instagram:
How does stop-motion animation work?

One minute of stop-motion is 1,440 photos, and a good animator makes about four seconds a week. Nudge a clay chai-wallah frame by frame, look inside his metal skeleton, make him talk with swapped mouths, ghost the last frames with onion skin, and plan your own film on a phone.

→ Stop-motion: move a puppet a few millimetres, take one photo, and repeat.
→ One minute of film needs 1,440 frames. A good animator makes about four seconds a week.
→ Inside the puppet is a metal skeleton with stiff ball-and-socket joints.
→ Screws or magnets in the feet hold it steady, and a rig holds it in mid-air.
→ To make a puppet talk, animators swap in a new mouth shape for each sound.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/stopmotionclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does stop-motion animation work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
One minute of stop-motion is 1,440 photos, and a good animator makes about four seconds a week. Nudge a clay chai-wallah frame by frame, look inside his metal skeleton, make him talk with swapped mouths, ghost the last frames with onion skin, and plan your own film on a phone.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/stopmotionclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/stopmotionclear

In this video:
• One frame at a time. An animator moves a puppet a few millimetres, steps away, and the camera takes one photo.
• Puppets and armatures. Inside a puppet is a metal skeleton with ball-and-socket joints, tightened so they hold any pose.
• Faces that talk. Animators match about eight mouth shapes to the voice, frame by frame.
• Onion skin and flicker. Frame-grab software shows the live camera view with the last frames ghosted over it, so the animator can check spacing: a falling ball should speed up.
• Not only puppets. Cut-out paper on multiplane glass (Lotte Reiniger, 1926), pixilated people (Norman McLaren's Neighbours, 1952), dancing matchsticks (Dadasaheb Phalke, 1915) and sand on a light box (Caroline Leaf, 1969) all use the same trick.
• Make your own. A phone on a tripod, a lamp and some clay are enough.
